title: One Granth for all
hookLine: every stream bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib

lines: BLUE ROBES, WHITE CLOTHES, NEW TUNES.
LOOK AT THE FRONT OF THE ROOM.
cards: Go back over the streams this block has visited. A Nihang camp, blue robes and steel. An Udasi dera with its quiet ascetics.
A Nirmala house of learning. A taksal where students drill every vowel. A Namdhari gathering in white.
A sangat in New Mexico or Toronto singing in a mix of Punjabi and English. Different clothes, different tunes, different arguments. Now look at the front of each room.
Raised a little, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: the same book. Today is that book, at the center of the streams.

teach.h: GURUS AND SAINTS IN ONE VOLUME.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib holds the hymns of Sikh Gurus alongside saints from other backgrounds, Kabir, Ravidas, Farid and more, gathered into one volume and sung in ragas.
Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave it the Guruship.
Since then it is not treated as a book on a shelf: it is installed each morning under a canopy, read aloud, waved over with a whisk, and laid to rest at night.
When one stream disagrees with another about diet, music, dress or the Dasam Granth, this is where both sides return. They bow to the same Guru.
Gurbani gives the reason in Guru Ram Das's words on Ang 982, here in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word; within the Word are all the nectars.
The Guru is not a person anyone can claim for their side.

teach.h: THE SAME PAGES IN EVERY GURDWARA.
teach.b: It is the Word itself, open on the same pages in every gurdwara. That has a practical effect.
A Sikh walking into a gurdwara of a different stream, in another country, will find the same hymns and the same order of pages, and can sit down and follow along.

The Namdharis, too, who keep a living guru of their own, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and sing from it. The streams are many. The center is one book, and in each of those rooms, heads bow before it.

how: Across the Sikh streams the Guru Granth Sahib is installed under a canopy, read aloud and bowed to as Guru; Sikhs from any stream can follow the same hymns on the same pages in any gurdwara.

games.q: what does “one granth for all” mean?
o: each stream keeps its own edition of scripture
every Sikh stream bows to the same scripture
a plan to print the Granth in every language

s: the Sikh streams in this block each have their own scripture in place of the Guru Granth Sahib
they bow to the same Guru Granth Sahib.
the Granth holds hymns of saints from beyond the Sikh Gurus
Kabir, Ravidas, Farid and more sit beside the Gurus.
a Sikh visiting a gurdwara abroad can follow the same pages
the same hymns, the same order, in every gurdwara.

games.q: two streams of Sikhs disagree about music, dress and diet. where do both turn?
o: to the same Guru Granth Sahib.
to separate books of their own.
games.why: they bow to the same Guru. on Ang 982, Guru Ram Das says the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word.

practice: If you're near a gurdwara, you can go in, cover your head, and bow before the Guru Granth Sahib; if not, picture the book under its canopy and lower your head a little where you sit.
If you don't keep this faith, simply hold respect for a book people of many streams bow to; if you pray, rest on the Word, the Guru.

wordCard.voice: One Granth for all. Every stream of the panth bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib, the Word as Guru, open on the same pages in every gurdwara. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the Guru's Word, the hymns of the Granth.

carryVoice: Your line: one granth. The same pages lie open in every room, whatever the stream. Until tomorrow.
